blocks.x: I'll call you Al. Oh, I want you to. Okay. And we'll talk. He's going to play a little bit, talk a bit. And those of you in high school will be led out by our college, we have some college boys in charge, showing where to go.

I think make the Coo sound exactly like a Coo, like a 2. Of course you would never use it that slow. You'd only use it when a single tongue becomes too fast. That's the regular Tukutu. Now the triple tongue would be Tukutu Tukutu Tukutu. Mr. Jansen, I've heard this many, many times. Where trumpet players will say to the conductor, could you take it a little faster because it's too hard to double tongue at the speed. I have never had this trumbler. I don't understand. Is it different on a brass instrument? No, seriously, I...
Sometimes we feel the tempo is too slow for double tongue or triple tongue. In other words, when you get to an in-between tempo, you know what I mean? Yes.
You don't know what to use, double... Oh, yes, you're right at that borderline there.
Yeah, yeah.
Yes, but can you still double tongue it if it's a little too slow?
Yes, yes it can be done, sure. In fact, Harry Glenn's human. Yes, sure. He had a very poor single tongue. Well, I don't have the greatest, I'll admit it. He's going to double with everything.
Yes, yes. Many things, I double and triple tongue slow.
That was single tongue.
But I single tongueed it faster than I double tongueed it. What I'm trying to prove is that it can be done slow.
Right. I'm going to play something for you and then I'll explain why I'm playing it.
Thanks.
You familiar with that?

Sure. The rage flag. Well, this actually happened. I was working on a small radio station in New York, 1934 and 35. And we had an orchestra of about 10 men. Trumpet, three saxes, violin, cello. And this one night, every night we used to do Empire Gold or something. But before that there was a rave track call, done live by the trumpet player. The trumpet player was late. And Louis Katzman, who was a conductor very good one I'll never forget. He says, man, if this guy doesn't show up. I says, look, I'll do it on sax. What's the difference? They won't know it. So I had to do it on sax. I'll never forget that.

I think, you know, you had so many years of experience with Paul Whiteman, starting with Toscanini. Right. Why don't you people ask some questions? He has some terrific stories. We just came off of a radio show with Roy Roberts on WSMB, what, an hour or two ago? Oh, 11 to 1131. You know, the nut to nut and stuff sort of thing. And yesterday we were on WWL. And Mr. Gavro has some marvelous things, stories that will help you even musically. Yes. Sure. So why don't you fire away? Start with the Paul Whiteman area if you want to. Make it a music history class, huh?

Well, I suppose I'll tell them about the Toscanini incident. Yeah, come on. Well, you've heard of Paul LaValle, the band leader, Paul LaValle. Well, I was working an ice show. Sonya Henney and Arthur Works opened up this ice show. They weren't in the show. Like the shows that you see now on tour, the ice shows, Holiday on the Ice and so forth. All right. Well, we opened the original. And Paul LaValle at that time was at NBC. And he says, Al, he says, how would you like to go with Toscanini? I said, gee, I don't know. I says, I played bass clarinet with Whiteman. I'm not afraid of the parts, but how about the bass clap? I didn't know the bass clap, you know. Well, I knew the bass clap, but only to transpose it like a cello part, a tone higher. But in the symphony, when they write the bass clarinet, they write it in your class. They write it in your key. In other words, the second space is a C, right? Now, if it's a cello part, I would have to play a D because this is B flat instrument. But they don't write it that way. They write, when they write a C, it's already transposed for you. So therefore, you play a C on your bass clarinet. So anyway, I took out my books. I have these recording books with passages from the Puccini operas and so forth. And man, I'm practicing up on them, you know. And Dr. Frank Black was a big conductor. He says, Al, you're playing these a tone too high. He says, you're playing the mezzo soprano, I believe. So they had to write me the Tristani's oldie in my key, right. So anyway, I says, I'm not worrying about that in a few weeks. I'll get it down. So here I go on stage 8H. I'll never forget it. Toscanine is in the audience. Dr. Frank Black and H. Leopold's Bittani. And there I am sitting on this big stage, all in all, with the bass clarinet, playing off of this and playing off of that. Well, I want to tell you. If you ever got scared, I was scared. I was scared because here was the master, you know. But I played a few things written out and within two weeks, you know what I did? I played smart. You have to play smart. You just go out and get yourself trombone books, bassoon books, anything in bass clef, and you just take it easy. And within a couple of weeks, I knew the bass clef. That's one story of my life. I was there two and a half years. I'd like to play something for you from the Tristan and Isolde solo. Now, if you notice, I played this all in that same register, in the same neighborhood. If you played... Of course, I do it pretty smooth, you know. But still, it's a different change. So, I decided to keep it all in this register. I have to tell you this. It's not bragging because it actually happened. We were doing a Red Cross benefit at Carnegie Hall with Toscanini. And this was the first time we had played this after I joined the symphony. And we played it and Misha Misha Koffer was the concertmaster. After I got through playing it, Toscanini looks down to Misha Misha Koffer and says, like this, you know. I thought to myself, oh my God, what happened? I thought I played it well. So, after Misha comes to me, doing a five-minute break, he says, you know what the old band said about you? He said, that's the first time we ever heard that passage played in tune. This is the truth. Because when you jump to the C, it's have to be sharp. The C is have to be sharp on the bass clarinet. But here, if you tune them right, you have better control. So, I thought I'd pass that along if you could ever play it, try and conquer it this way. Then, let's see the other part. Oh yes, the high notes. I use my own, how many bass clarinet players here? Many? None here.
One today in the back, wait a minute.
Would you demonstrate the play the Grove major you did last night? Yes.
Hmm. Yes, what I tried to bring out is I don't use this B-flat.

I go the hard way and use this one because it's safe. Sometimes this may not cover. I don't keep mine covered anyway because I don't use it. I'd rather have play in there to make sure that this comes down. So, I use the side B-flat. If this is leaking, even if it isn't leaking that much, the note won't speak. Where here, you're safe because this is just a key that you press down. Then, on the high register, I use different fingerings. There's a passage in, I believe it's American in Paris, where the bass clarinet goes.
I use an open T, a regular open T for the high T. . I think we have some pianists.
We have some people from music school. How many pianists are here today? Pianists? Pianists? Could you tell us something about Gershwin? Because he...

Well, I didn't know Gershwin. Yes, I worked with him once with Paul Weitman, but it was a short-lived thing, you know. Well, as far as I'm concerned, Gershwin never wrote a bad piece of music. I think everything Gershwin wrote was gorgeous, absolutely gorgeous. From his concerto for doubles, concerto for nap.
Yeah.
But he and Weitman made each other, actually, because when the Rhapsody and Boo was written, that's when they both really branched out.
All right, we have just a few more minutes. Any questions? Can we hear... Can I ask some questions? Yeah, sure. What problems do you encounter in the altissimo range of the saxophone?

Well, I have my own fingerings. And, of course, a lot of that depends on the reed and yourself. It's stoke again. Now, here, as I mentioned last night, we're low climate here, right? Damp. The reeds are apt to get a little softer here. When I go back to New York, they'll play just slightly harder. But if I took these same reeds to Colorado at Gunnison, where it's... I don't know how many feet up, they would be hard. Absolutely hard-blowing. And those are the problems when you travel. You try to pick out enough reeds, you know, different grades of strength. But the high notes has a lot to do with the covering of the horn also. Now, the high F is coming out today, see? Because last night, evidently, the reed was wetter and my lip was... But that's a very hard one. Yes. That was a good question you asked. If you... Here, you also have to think high. That's what they'll have to do. So when I try to teach it, have them play chromatic. But they still will do that until they get used to it. Let's just do it.
It's just a question of practice.
But the way to get up there, I still say from the previous notes, the sort of slur up there, and keep your throat going. Same as if you're going for a high note on the clarinet. Yes.
Do you use the same finger as you use the C?
High F, yes. That's right. Well, sometimes if the C is flat, I'll use it. But it doesn't seem to be good for the high F. Well, I have two. These here, this, and this. This is a little sharper.

That's very difficult. Thank you. Thank you. I've been working on it, but it's so windy, you know. It's very windy. Uh, Mr. Karuba, Mr. Millman, I'm sure. They have to leave? I'm willing to say. It's up to you.
Well, I had thought if it wouldn't be an imposition, some of the saxophone majors would like a little conclave.
So I had promised by not to have an interview here.
Right.

And then we could stay here. Yes. We want to have an interview here. We want to have an interview here. Right. And then we could stay here. Yes. We want to have an interview here. We have an interview here. Right, and then we can stay here. And we can dismiss the others? Yes, we'd like to dismiss the others. Now we have, for those, how many students you have taking back to each other? I'll be with Mr. Gallo. No, we're locally. Mr. Piliacos. Alec, would you take them back to the music school? We have all the rooms posted for each one. Now may we have a show of hands on the percussionists. How many percussionists do we have here today? Okay. We follow Mr. Kaufman. He'll take you to the field house. Suppose we...
In New Orleans.
Well, I started my professional career, actually in New Orleans. I played a little in Birmingham with makeup bands, you know.
Travel groups or spots?
Yeah, I went to Pensacola with a group. But my big job actually came here in New Orleans, the Orphan Theater.
It was an art movie.
Yes.
What was his answer?
Can you read that? Yeah. I think it was November roughly of 1928.
And when did you get to start playing with that call? What was his name?

What was his name? Spring of 1936. What was his name? Funny thing, I picked up... Who was his name? I tried many clarinets at the factory. And I came down to three clarinets. So they sent them to me later. So they sent them to me later. I didn't take them with me. They sent them to me. And they were different numbers. And this number... I like this clarinet, but I also like the number. 1936.
I don't know. I don't know. Just for luck, I'll take this. Sentimental reasons. Yeah. Sentimental reasons.
Oh, is that all I see?
That's specially made with the gold keys for you, Al? Yes. Gold play. Gold play. Yes. How long have you been playing at him? Since when?
Well, I started clarinet when I was seven years old. My father taught me. He was a clarinetist also.
Did you always want to be a musician?
Yes.
Always.

From the age of five, I used to take my father's clarinet, if you want to add that. We lived on a Louisiana farm, a strawberry section. And I used to take his clarinet while he was out in the field, and he'd hear, you know, squeak and squawk. So he'd come in and he'd say, son, you're a little too young, Ed, and you might hurt the clarinet, you know. And this went on several months and a long time. You know, he'd hide the clarinet with some heart. I'd go and find it. You know how kids are, you know. Huckleberry Finn. And he actually started me when I was seven years old.
Well, how did you get your breakfast from Paul White?

Well, when the theater closed in 1933, when the Orphean closed with Vortemul, rather, the other way with Vortemul, I decided to go to New York. In New York, I stopped in Philadelphia first. I don't know how long you want this story to be, but you can always cut it down, right? Oh, John. I stopped, yes. I stopped in Philadelphia to see a trumpet player from New Orleans. To be exact, his name was Danny Rhyne. R-Y-N. Danny Rhyne. And Philadelphia, I found out he was working in Atlantic City. He greeted me beautifully, but there was nothing he could do because he was just a sideman with this band that he was playing with. But he did tell me to go to Atlantic City to see a fiddle player that was also from New Orleans. At that time, he was with the George Olsen band. And perhaps that he could do something for me. His name was Adrian Fresh. He was some fiddler. Oh, my goodness.

This was the one Sal Franzella used to talk about. Instead of talking about anyone, he would always talk about your ability as a saxophonist and clarinet. Is that the one he had great admiration for your performance and playing? Adrian Fresh?

Adrian Fresh? Possibly. He's probably deceased now. But when I got to Atlantic City, George Olsen had left the night before. So I was more or less stuck. But I saw that next door to the hotel that Olsen was in, Isham Jones. I-A-I-S-H-A-M. Isham Jones. He was some composer. He was a multi-millionaire when he passed away at Turkey Ranch. He wrote all of those beautiful tunes like Swinging Down the Lane and things like that. Anyway, I went to see his manager and he was interested in what I had to say. He gave me an audition the following day. And Jones actually didn't have any need for me because he had five saxes. But he liked my playing and so forth and he added me on as an extra. He was just to do a few solos here and there, you know. And I was with the band. See, I wish I had those records I'd record. I recorded two things with Isham Jones. Dallas Man and doing Uptown Lowdown. They collect design. I don't even have them. Well, anyway, I was with the Jones band around four months. This Atlantic City and between Atlantic City and a tour of New England states. About four months. Then we landed in New York. That's when he had to let me go because I didn't have a union card. That's what the six months are. I couldn't work steady, see. He went into the Commodore Hotel. So he said, Al, there's nothing I can do. I said, I know, I understand. So then I start doing little jobs with different offices and so forth. And what you call here spot jobs. You still call them spot jobs or club dates? Club dates. Club dates, yeah. Yeah, we call them spot jobs. Years ago they were spot jobs and now it's club dates. And I got an offer to go to one of the small radio stations in New York. I worked there roughly two years, 34, 30, roughly two years. Yes, to the spring of 36 because that's where Whiteman comes in. And one of the arrangers for Rubinoff, who was a big man at the time, says, Al, Whiteman is looking for a first alto man. So I told him, I says, well, if Mr. Whiteman wishes to hear me, to tune in this radio station, which was WRNS to be exact. And there we used to play solos all day long. We used to work six days a week. And every show we did a solo with the accordion or with piano, you know. And I told him roughly when it was and Whiteman heard me play. I made sure that I, this one particular time I played clarinet and sax, you know, to give him an idea. And he was impressed and he made me on offer and I accepted it. This was the spring of 1936. And that June we went to the famous Casa Manana in Fort Worth. Billy Rose's Casa Manana. We spent two summers there, 36 and 37. And I was with Whiteman all these years. We toured the whole country from coast to coast. You know, I still have my hotel receipts. Probably not. Well, I'm a bug in keeping things, you know. Because I did a concert in Lorain, Ohio about five years ago. And I remembered the hotel and I said, when I get back home, I'm going to check it. I went all through my hotel receipts and the ad was Lorain, Ohio, 1940. Well, the Whiteman band is banded May 30th to be exact. 1940. This was the organized band, of course. And that June we went to Hollywood to do the... Was there a week? Well, I'm sorry. Four. He took four musicians. Trumpet, banjo, myself, and... What was the fourth one? To do the strike up the band picture with Mickey Rooney and Judy Garland. You went to Hollywood to? Right. In June. June of 1940. They still show it on television. It's a very good thing. We had a few shots in it. I have seen it. After the picture, that was the end of the band entirely, you know. And Whiteman, of course, retired for about a year and a half, but he reorganized the band. But by that time, I went to NBC with Toscanini. That was 1942, June of 1942. Toscanini and Leopold Stokowski. At that time, they were sharing the podium alternating week and week. And Stokowski was a very big name then. He still is a big name. That man is very old. But he's got the New York American Symphony he conducts. As a matter of fact, they just went to Albany. A lot of opera stars, did you read about it? Because they're complaining about tearing down that metropolitan. Right. It's a sin, you know. That's a landmark, just like some of your buildings here. But, you know, the big corporations come in. They don't care about a landmark. They're thinking of green paper, you know. So, I hope that it stays. Acoustically, they say it's wonderful. You just can't duplicate it.
What are they planning on putting there? Are they planning on building Newwood?
Oh, sure. One of these modern skyscrapers, you know, like you see all over the country. Parkman building, I believe. Possible.
Office space.

Yeah, sure. For every building you've got here, we built 15 there. This is no exaggeration. Park Avenue is just nothing but steel buildings. All your big companies. So, anyway, I was with NBC for about two years and a half. Toscanini. Then I left and started to freelance. And, oh, God. That's when I was doing Percy Faith's Carnation Milk Hour. And Antonini, who's with CBS, conductor there. And various recordings, various movies.
Could you name some of those in the story?

Yeah, I'm trying to think of one big movie we made with Mel Ferrer. Lost Boundaries. Hey, Howard. How you doing? Great, man. Have you seen Lost Boundaries? No, I haven't seen that. Once in a while. Well, it had to do with this family up in New England that were half colored, you know, and they were passing as white. So, it's a very good story. Nothing wrong with it. But the score was very good. I did quite a bit of alto work and clarinet and bass clarinet. You hear it here and there. You know, they show Harlem and so forth. Lost Boundaries is one of the movies. And then, of course, that lasted about three, four years. And then I joined the ABC staff, American Broadcasting Company. Already that's spring of 47 when I joined there. And freelance at the same time.
When did you start working with Sylvia? You are a clarinet.

Well, I've been playing Sylvia instruments actually since 1927. Clarinet. Matter of fact, Howard sold me the first one. You remember? I bought the metal, the silver clarinet. Sure. Then I didn't care for it and I switched over to the wooden. Okay.
And, Scott, I know you have a lot of things to do.
That's all right. And, uh, I'll tell you what you can mention. The movies are not out yet. We scored two movies and the music is great on both of them. One is called Bridie of the Grand Canyon.
Isn't that about a horse? Yes.

What did you read about it? When I was little. Yes, that's right. But it's supposed to be a very good picture and I imagine it's a clean one for a change. Yeah. The scenery is great. The score is very good. It's modern but... Who wrote the score? Oh, born... Not Herman, you didn't know? No, no. I'll have to think of the fellow's name. Young fellow. About 30, 35. But the music is good. I have a few solos here and there. Did you do any with Andre Previn and his score?
Oh, he's got to answer that.

No. Never worked with him. He's great though. The other movie we just did about six weeks ago, Rings Around the World. You remember the circus show that Don Amici had? Mm-hmm. Well, it's on that style. What they've done, they've gone to France, Spain, and all over the world and filmed different acts in circuses, you know. But Don Amici narrates very little. 85% of the picture is exposed to music. The rest is action. Jack Belasco did this and he's got some beautiful themes going. That man is just going crazy, he and his wife, because they want to put the soundtrack on an album. And if just one tune hits, you know, you can clean up on it. He's thrilled to death. He's a very good writer. So those are the two movies that I was in recently, rather the music, you know.
Al, did you ever have any small little jazz groups?

Yes, I formed one when I did the Columbia album. This was 1951. I had 25 arrangements made. The Chic, Out of Nowhere, After You're Gone, Lover. And the group lasted two weeks. I had a manager, but he didn't book nightclubs. He says, I don't book nightclubs. Do you think the recording?
December 54, Ralph Herman did the concerto for doubles for band because originally it was... 54? December 54. When did you record that? Well, no, we recorded it in 1948 I guess it was.
You sent me a concerto for doubles.
You sure? Really? I don't even remember.
I haven't.

Son of a gun. I'll play for you tomorrow night. Oh my God, it's a collector's item. I can go on and on. Take it on tape, that's all right. We got it. All right. Whiteman commissioned this for me and the reason it was called concerto for doubles in the band, I played alto, clarinet, and bass clarinet. So we had a special broadcast one night where I played the three instruments and I did like oodles and oodles on sax, I did the Flight of the Bumblebee on clarinet. And I believe I did something on bass clarinet, I can't remember what it was. But this was to give the composers an idea of my capabilities and so forth and to write around that. Write them difficult, write them easy, make it hard, you know. So we received roughly about 18 concertos. And believe me when I tell you this, this can be verified by some of the boys at ABC. I was on a go seven days a week because I had to prepare every concerto and get it under my fingers with any reason. Because we had to try it. If you can't play something halfway decent, Whiteman would have never been able to tell how it sounded. So we tried some and if it didn't work out, he says let's try the other movement. And if he liked it, we went through it. Well anyway, we went through about 18 of them. And we finally got down to four concertos that we liked. And this one broadcast, I did two on a half hour broadcast, two on another one. And brother, they were tough. I have all the records of them, you know. They were very difficult. So where was I now? What were we talking about the concerto? The concerto notes. Oh yeah, but I went through it. 1950. But the record. Yes, we recorded the concerto for doubles. Manna albums. And here's the first thing that happens. Ralph Herman had been writing for Manna albums, you know, arranging for the singers and so forth. He says, Al, they would like to try something different. They would like to record the concerto for doubles. Fine. We started at midnight at Carnegie Hall with about a 50 piece orchestra. We went to six in the morning. The Oodles and Noodles was done at quarter of six in the morning. Honest to goodness. And in those days, there wasn't any tape. If you broke a record, you had to start the whole thing over again. Well, we made two, three takes. Oodles and Noodles, we made two takes. Because we were running short of time. Well, the album sold pretty good. And after a while, I asked for royalties. And, well, the accountant will be in and so forth. I got a check for about $240. Ralph Herman was conducting at the radio station in Milwaukee. That's where he's from. He says, we'll send Ralph's check. Well, he never got the check. Finally, one partner bought out the other partner. There were four of us, incidentally. We signed it. These are fags. We each put up $1,350 each to make this thing. It cost close to roughly $6,000. That's all. One partner buys the other partner. He puts it under a different label, ARCO label. Then he finally skips to Miami. And if you look at your musician's journal or the local 802 or international musician, you will notice Irving Berman, unfair list, Manor Records, unfair list. Ralph Herman can't even get his masters back. This is what's a heartbreaker. So anyway, about the Columbia album. In 1955, I started to do the concerts. And by that time, they discontinued the Columbia album. This is where they should have kept it up because the kids were asking, where can I get the Columbia album? I said, it's been discontinued. Jack Federson, who's the president now, wrote to Mitch Miller, why don't you release it? Nothing. Now this is 11 years ago. They have the masters right there. It's a sin that money is going to waste. I'm losing money. They're losing money. And they've got the masters there. I worked hard on that album. Have you heard it? The little one, the Columbia contrast? I did Liza, Dark Eyes. The name of the record is? Saxophone Contrast. Contrast. Yeah, Saxophone Contrast.
That's the one with the picture of the saxophone on the cover.

Yeah, red dots. Yeah, I have that. Red and white. You have that. Yeah. Alt V, the violin solo. Right. Dark Eyes, the charred eyes. Liza and... Indian Summer, Summertime. You get enough kids to write to Mitch Miller out, but he'd release it. He'd see that. Yes. You'd have to get a good manager, too, to open this thing up. See, what's terrible about it is that they have the masters and the records to be sold. It's just a sin having it lay there. And if you're offered to buy, goodness knows what they want. What a fortune.
Mr. Caleduro, who was it that I called you the Triple Threat Instrumentl?
Oh, that was Selma. Mr. Selma?
No, no.

Jack Fetterson. Oh, Jack Fetterson. Ah, forget her. F-E-double-D-E-R-S-E-N. S-E-N. He's now the president. He, Jack Fetterson, Bundy told me back in the 30s, he says Fetterson someday, he loved Fetterson, he says he is going to end up president of Selma in this country, and he certainly did.
And Fetterson is president of Selma? Becquard? He is president of Selma?
He is president of Selma Company now.
And he started calling you the Triple Threat Instrumentl?
Yes. Anything to do with Triple Tongue you think might have had, or just for the three instruments?

Well, the three instruments. Three instruments. See, the three instruments. Oh, I know what I forgot about the concerto for doubles. Yeah, yeah. The whole idea was that you doubled on three instruments. Weidman had that idea.
And that can't be obtained at all?

Becquard? Oh, God, no. You see, sometimes we miss out on ourselves. I could buy the records at that time at distributors' price, $2.19, but who thought of buying two, three hundred albums? The same way with Columbia. You think, oh, I'll wait until next month. By that time they're gone. The company goes broke. Now this has been going on, Howard, in the record industry for years. Bernie Green, who conducted the Sid Caesar Show, he is a tremendous composer. This man has ideas. He can write anything. Spike Jonze style anything. He used to do the Henry Morgan Show, you know the comedian, and used to write funny things. He recorded something on a high class Spike Jonze. It was funny, but in good taste. Ray Cricera, Carnival of Venice, I did Saxophobia, and then he wrote a thing called Idol, which he uses as a theme for the U.S. Steel Show. And he decided to make a clarinet quintet out of it. It's published by Boosie Hawks, I think. Five clarinets. Beautiful.
And what name?

I-D-Y-L-L. I-D-Y-L-L. Yeah, that's it. It was originally a violin theme for this show we did on Love Scene, you know. Now, that was in the album too. The album is called More Than You Can Stand, San Francisco Label. San Francisco Label is just a label that somebody makes up, like you can make one and, you know. Call it the Karuba Label. Exactly. That's all it is. The records, they sold a few. The company goes broke. Bernie didn't do anything with it. This goes on all the time.
Mr. Gallador, I served my own time at 4 o'clock class. So, I thank you very much. I think you have enough there to choose from.
Thank you very much.
Fine.

Thank you. Pleasure. Al, I know we're running a little show. I see how somebody's going to take you home to the hotel. You don't have to call a cab. Good, yeah. Could you just, something of my saxophone majors here have some questions. Yes. Longin, anything you would like to add?
Well, let's see. Well, Charlie had one thing. We heard you last night do a gliss from G. G. From G. On a sax? On a saxophone.
Yeah, well that was in that piece that I played. It was really from D to high F. That's all it was.
This is, your palm that you took?
Yes. Well, it was just the coordination of how you lift the keys and you throw them.

You go out and the same out. We were wondering how to do it because it's hard, it's hard getting through this G register. But once you get past it, it's fairly easy. You can do it for a, once in a while we can get it. Yes. But it's getting through this little register which gives us the palm.
